forces: Two violins, viola and two cellos
performers: Isaac Stern, Alexander Schneider, violins; Milton Katims, viola; Pablo Casals, Paul Tortelier, cellos
intro: The Adagio of Schubert’s String Quintet in C major, D. 956, opens with three inner voices playing while a violin and a pizzicato cello frame them; an F-minor middle section follows, and the opening returns altered. Pablo Casals and his Prades colleagues perform.

sections.label: A · melody in three voices, plucked cello
sections.mNote: Second violin, viola and first cello sustain the melody.

sections.label: B · F minor, violin and cello duet
sections.mNote: Bowed bass and off-beat inner strings accompany the duet.

sections.label: A′ · E major, demisemiquavers in second cello
sections.mNote: The second cello plays running demisemiquavers beneath the returning melody.

sections.label: Coda · F minor inflection before final E major
sections.mNote: The middle section’s key, F minor, returns in the last three bars.

cues.title: Opening melody, inner voices
cues.text: The second violin, viola and first cello play a slow melody in E major. Around them, the first violin plays short, dotted phrases and the second cello plucks the bass.
cues.evidence: Schubert’s Werke, Series IV, No. 1 (Breitkopf & Härtel, 1890), Adagio opening; Misha Donat describes the inner melody, first-violin phrases and pizzicato bass in his 2012 note. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W6016_67864
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Probst, 2 October 1828
cues.text: On 2 October 1828 Schubert, then thirty-one, wrote to the Leipzig publisher Heinrich Albert Probst offering three piano sonatas, Heine songs and a new quintet. The quintet was about to be tried out. The letter is Schubert’s only mention of the work.
cues.evidence: Schubert to Probst, 2 October 1828, quoted in Misha Donat’s programme note; the letter is Schubert’s only mention of the quintet (Egon Voss, preface to the Henle Urtext edition HN 812, 2006, citing Deutsch, Schubert: Die Dokumente seines Lebens, 1964, p. 540). The work remains unpublished until 1853. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W6016_67864

cues.title: Jonathan Blumhofer on the Adagio, 2024
cues.text: The composer Jonathan Blumhofer found this Adagio closely related to the slow movement of Schubert’s B♭ major piano sonata. He wrote that its nocturnal mood foreshadows later movements by Mahler and Bartók.
cues.evidence: Jonathan Blumhofer, programme note on Schubert’s String Quintet in C major (2024): https://www.jonathanblumhofer.com/writings/program-notes/schubert-string-quintet-in-c-major/

cues.title: Middle section in F minor
cues.text: The music moves to F minor, a semitone above E, fortissimo. The second cello changes to the bow, and the first violin and first cello play a long melody together. The inner parts accompany them with off-beat chords.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1890), Adagio middle section; Misha Donat describes the F-minor duet, syncopated inner accompaniment and active second cello. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W6016_67864
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Violin and cello in octaves
cues.text: The first violin and first cello play the melody in octaves, set wide apart. Beneath them the second cello plays an accompaniment, so the two cellos have different parts.
cues.evidence: Misha Donat’s programme note identifies violin and cello in octaves in the slow movement’s middle section and describes the second cello’s accompaniment. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W6016_67864
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, Vienna, 1850
cues.text: The first known public performance took place in Vienna on 17 November 1850, twenty-two years after Schubert’s death. The work was published in 1853. Schubert’s manuscript is lost, and the print is the only source.
cues.evidence: Egon Voss, preface to the Henle Urtext edition HN 812 (2006): the Hellmesberger Quartet, with Josef Stransky, plays the quintet at the Vienna Musikverein on 17 November 1850; the autograph score is missing and the Spina print of 1853 is the only source. IMSLP gives the same performance date and the 1853 Spina first edition. https://www.henle.de/en/String-Quintet-C-major-op.-post.-163-D-956/HN-812 https://imslp.org/wiki/String_Quintet,_D.956_(Schubert,_Franz)

cues.title: Brahms’s F minor string quintet, 1862
cues.text: In autumn 1862 Brahms sent Clara Schumann the first three movements of an F minor quintet for two violins, viola and two cellos, the ensemble Schubert used. He later destroyed it and recast the music for two pianos, then for piano quintet. The middle section of this Adagio is in F minor.
cues.evidence: Misha Donat, note on Brahms’s Piano Quintet, Op. 34 (Hyperion CDA67551, 2007): the first three movements sent to Clara in autumn 1862, for “the same ensemble that Schubert used for his great C major Quintet D956”; the string quintet destroyed; the two-piano sonata and then the piano quintet of 1864. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W8243_67551 The F-minor central section of the Adagio: Donat’s note on the Schubert, https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W6016_67864

cues.title: Return of E major
cues.text: E major returns. The three inner players take up their broad melody again, while the second cello now plays running demisemiquavers and exchanges flourishes with the first violin.
cues.evidence: Misha Donat’s note describes the first-violin and second-cello dialogue around the unchanged inner melody. The demisemiquavers are identified in the Adagio account at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_Quintet_(Schubert); https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W6016_67864.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Casals at Prades
cues.text: Pablo Casals made the small French town of Prades his home. Its first festival, in 1950, was devoted to Bach. The 1952 festival, recorded by Columbia and heard here, was the first given entirely to chamber music.
cues.evidence: Columbia Masterworks LP sleeve notes (Internet Archive item lp_casals-festival-at-prades-third-series-qui_franz-schubert-isaac-stern-alexander-schne): the 1950 Bach festival, the recordings made at the Festival of 1952, and the third festival as the first devoted entirely to chamber music. https://archive.org/details/lp_casals-festival-at-prades-third-series-qui_franz-schubert-isaac-stern-alexander-schne

cues.title: Percy Scholes on chamber music
cues.text: In The Oxford Companion to Music, Percy Scholes found “an intimacy” in the best chamber music “that comes from the impression of a conversation amongst the participants”. His poetic definition of it was “The Music of Friends”. The Columbia sleeve for this recording quoted him.
cues.evidence: Percy Scholes, The Oxford Companion to Music, entry “Chamber Music”: “There is an intimacy about the best chamber music that comes from the impression of a conversation amongst the participants. A poetic definition of it is ‘The Music of Friends’.” Quoted in the Columbia Masterworks LP sleeve notes (Internet Archive item lp_casals-festival-at-prades-third-series-qui_franz-schubert-isaac-stern-alexander-schne). https://archive.org/details/lp_casals-festival-at-prades-third-series-qui_franz-schubert-isaac-stern-alexander-schne

cues.title: Tully Potter in The Strad
cues.text: Reviewing this recording in The Strad, Tully Potter called Tortelier’s pizzicatos in the Adagio “superb”. He wrote that “groans from Casals” “only increase the tension”, and he heard “tremendous thrust” in the central section.
cues.evidence: Tully Potter, review of the July 1952 Prades recording of the quintet (reissued on Minuet 428419), The Strad, December 2016: “groans from Casals only increase the tension”. https://www.thestrad.com/schubert-string-quintet-in-c-major-d956-schumann-piano-trio-no1-in-d-minor/4804.article

cues.title: F minor in the final bars
cues.text: The last three bars turn briefly to F minor, the key of the middle section, before closing in E major.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1890), Adagio, final three bars; harmonic close described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_Quintet_(Schubert).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: E major to F minor, fortissimo
transitions.from: A · melody in three voices, plucked cello
transitions.to: B · F minor, violin and cello duet
transitions.how: E major breaks off and the music moves to F minor, fortissimo. The second cello changes from plucked bass to bowed motion. The first violin and first cello play the long melody in octaves, with syncopated chords between them.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1890), Adagio, p. 18; Misha Donat’s description of the middle section. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W6016_67864

transitions.title: Separated chords return to E major
transitions.from: B · F minor, violin and cello duet
transitions.to: A′ · E major, demisemiquavers in second cello
transitions.how: The F-minor passage ends in quiet, separated chords. These lead back to E major and the sustained inner melody. The first violin and second cello now exchange quick flourishes around the other three players.
transitions.evidence: Misha Donat’s programme note describes the faltering transition and varied reprise. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W6016_67864

transitions.title: The F-minor chord returns
transitions.from: A′ · E major, demisemiquavers in second cello
transitions.to: Coda · F minor inflection before final E major
transitions.how: In the last three bars, F minor again briefly interrupts E major. The five strings return to the home key at once and close softly.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1890), Adagio, final three bars on p. 25. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_Quintet_(Schubert)

source.title: Schubert, Streichquintett C-dur, Franz Schubert’s Werke, Serie IV No. 1 (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel, 1890, plate F.S. 22)
source.locator: IMSLP #885759, second movement, Adagio, printed pages 17–25. The two cello parts are grouped together here. The last three bars appear above the Scherzo on page 25.

timeline.note: Second violin, viola and first cello sustain the melody between dotted first-violin phrases and plucked second cello.
First violin and first cello play in octaves, fortissimo in F minor; the second cello plays a driving figure beneath them.
The five strings play quiet, separated chords as the music returns to E major.
The inner melody returns in E major, surrounded by first-violin flourishes and running second-cello demisemiquavers.
A brief F-minor chord gives way to the E-major ending.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Isaac Stern (violin), Alexander Schneider (violin), Milton Katims (viola), Pablo Casals (cello), Paul Tortelier (cello)
fields.note: The Internet Archive item lists these five performers as creators; the Substack essay assigns the roles and calls the recording a Columbia release made at the Prades Festival. Which cellist plays the first cello part and which the second is not stated in any source consulted.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The performing edition is not identified. The Internet Archive file names print the posthumous opus number 163 for the work, which Schubert’s catalogue gives as D. 956.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.value: 1952 (the Casals Festival at Prades); one secondary source says July
fields.note: The LP sleeve notes say the recordings were made in Prades during the Casals Festival of 1952; the Discogs master release and a 6moons review also say 1952. Only the Substack essay by John Buxton gives a month, July 1952, so the month is not treated as established, and the day is not stated.

fields.note: The sleeve notes say the recordings were made in Prades during the Casals Festival of 1952. Substack says the recording was made in Prades, France during the Prades Festival; Discogs and 6moons say it was recorded at the Prades Festival in 1952.

fields.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.

fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis).
fields.note: The Internet Archive item gives publication date 1953 and the Discogs master release gives the year 1953, so the 50-year European term expired before the 2013 extension. The item carries no licence statement; no US public-domain basis is claimed, and the 1953 date is not independently verified against a label image.
alts: Pre-1963 European public domain — territorial basis, publication 1953.
No licence or rights statement on the Internet Archive item.

composer.epithet: Composer who at seventeen wrote a song for Gretchen with a spinning-wheel accompaniment and at thirty-one wrote music for two cellos.
facts: Vienna Stadtkonvikt, 1808–13; composition lessons with Antonio Salieri
School assistant; tutor to the Esterházy daughters at Zseliz in 1818 and 1824; independent composer
The singer Vogl, the poets Schober and Mayrhofer, the painter Schwind, Josef von Spaun
More than 600 songs; symphonies, chamber music, piano sonatas and duets, masses and stage works

quote.text: I like these songs more than all the others, and you will come to like them too.
quote.source: Schubert to his friends about Winterreise, 1827, as Josef von Spaun later recalled; our translation

composer.background:
In the Schubert family quartet, Franz played the viola, his brothers the violins and his father the cello. He was born on 31 January 1797 in Himmelpfortgrund, a Viennese suburb, and grew up in his father’s schoolhouse. His father taught him violin, his brother Ignaz piano, and the parish musician Michael Holzer taught him further. At eleven he entered the imperial chapel choir and the Stadtkonvikt boarding school, where he played Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven in the school orchestra.

Salieri began teaching him composition in 1812. The next year Schubert left the boarding school, trained as a teacher and returned to his father’s classroom as an assistant. On 19 October 1814, aged seventeen, he wrote Gretchen am Spinnrade. In the piano part the right hand imitates the spinning wheel and the left hand the treadle, while Goethe’s Gretchen sings of her thoughts of Faust. At the point where she recalls his kiss, the accompaniment figure stops. The following year brought roughly 140 songs, among them Erlkönig, as well as church music, a symphony and works for the stage.
